text: When the applause ends, the room is still a room. The lights go out. The names on the walls remain. But the person goes home, carrying questions that achievement has not settled. What makes a life matter? What do we owe one another? And why does a voice from Galilee keep entering the conversation?

title:
THE QUESTION
THAT REMAINS
subtitle: A film about achievement, faith, doubt, and service

text: Christmas Eve, nineteen eighty-three. An American president addresses the nation. Ronald Reagan names a distinction at the heart of Christianity: admiration for a teacher, and faith in something more.
A president's conviction is a personal conviction. Office cannot turn it into proof. The question survives the speaker's rank. It asks something of a life that power, by itself, cannot answer.

For geneticist Francis Collins, the journey began beside a patient. In his own account, her faith unsettled his assumptions. He began to examine a question he had considered closed. This is a scientist describing a personal search. The method of a laboratory and the act of religious belief remain different things. His testimony brings us to the point where that search became particular.

He names a person. The Christian claim is that meaning can be encountered in a life: in words, actions, suffering, and the hope of resurrection. That claim invites examination. It also meets resistance.

title: The wound
subtitle: The objection deserves to be heard

text: In another interview, Stephen Fry is asked what he would say if confronted by God. His answer refuses consolation. He begins with the suffering of children.

The objection deserves more than an answering montage. No celebrated believer can make another person's suffering disappear. And no film can settle that argument by arranging faces on a screen. We can leave the wound visible. We can listen to what people do with it.

title: Forgiveness
subtitle: What do we do with suffering?

text: At Homeboy Industries, Jim Carrey speaks about pain, resentment, and forgiveness. He draws on Christ's suffering to speak about grace, and the possibility of a life beyond resentment. His subject is the practice of forgiveness.

In a separate conversation, Bono tells a different story. The language is explicitly a profession of faith. Asked about prayer, he makes his answer personal. These voices do not offer one interchangeable account. Each speaks from a particular life.

title: Victory
subtitle: What remains when the score is gone?

text: Success has its own vocabulary: the score, the record, the award. At his twenty-fifteen Most Valuable Player speech, Stephen Curry begins by giving thanks. For a moment, the language of achievement opens onto a question of identity.

Winning can describe what happened. It cannot contain everything a person is. And if worth depends on winning, what becomes of the injured, the forgotten, the person who never gets a place on the stage?

In February nineteen sixty-eight, Martin Luther King Junior preached about our hunger to be first. He called it the drum major instinct. His sermon turns toward Jesus, and toward a different measure of greatness. The desire to matter is redirected into service. The door is opened to everyone.

Service brings the question down to earth. Whose hunger do we notice? Whose burden do we share? At an Easter prayer breakfast in twenty-fifteen, Barack Obama speaks about the example of Jesus, then about the distance between that example and his own life.

The voices end. The work remains. A meal. An act of forgiveness. The courage to hear a difficult question without turning away. Belief and doubt have not become the same thing. Yet the invitation to examine a life is still here. Beyond the titles, beyond the applause, the question becomes our own.
